 The Best NAS for Plex in 2026 Has an Intel Chip With Quick Sync
Updated on

by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The best NAS for Plex has an Intel processor with Quick Sync, which Plex fully supports for converting 4K and HDR video. Our pick for most home libraries is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, a four-bay box with room for a growing collection. AMD boxes and the Synology DS925+ are weaker choices, since Plex only partly supports AMD graphics and the Synology has none.
Recommendation
 On a tighter budget, the two-bay UGREEN DXP2800 has the same Quick Sync engine. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a cheaper way to get four bays.
 A NAS for Plex needs two things: enough drive bays for the library, and a processor that can convert video on the fly when a TV, phone, or remote viewer cannot play a file as it is stored. The second part decides the purchase, because Plex supports hardware transcoding on Intel’s Quick Sync video engine, including HDR to SDR tone mapping, with no artificial cap on simultaneous streams. Its AMD support is unofficial and covers SDR video only. A NAS with no integrated graphics, such as Synology’s DS925+, does every conversion on its CPU cores.
 Six of the twelve NAS units below have Intel graphics that Plex fully supports, and all six come from UGREEN and TerraMaster. Prices below are list prices for the diskless box, the same figures as in our NAS comparison chart , so budget separately for hard drives.

 The DXP4800 Plus pairs four bays with an Intel chip that Plex fully supports, at a list price of $619.99. Four bays let you run RAID 5 with one drive’s worth of protection, which is the usual layout for a media library that will keep growing. The 12th-generation Pentium Gold 8505 scores about 70 percent higher than the N100 in budget boxes on PassMark’s CPU benchmark, so the CPU has room for Plex’s library scans, thumbnail generation, and a few Docker apps while Quick Sync handles the transcode. WunderTech’s July 2026 Plex roundup also names it the top pick. The rest of the box is 8GB of DDR5 that expands to 64GB, one 10GbE port and one 2.5GbE port, two M.2 slots, and a 128GB system SSD.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro has no native Plex package, so Plex runs as a Docker container that you set up yourself, and you have to give that container access to the graphics device before Quick Sync will work. UGREEN’s own Plex vs Jellyfin guide lists Plex as “Runs through Docker.” The DXP4800 Plus also drew about 24 watts at idle with four hard drives spinning in KitGuru’s test , or about 210 kWh a year for a box that never sleeps.
 The UGREEN DXP2800 brings Quick Sync to a two-bay budget

 The DXP2800 carries the same Quick Sync engine in an Intel N100, with 8GB of DDR5, two M.2 slots, and one 2.5GbE port, for $389.99. Lon.TV tested an N100 mini PC as a Plex server and found that a 4K VP9 video and a Blu-ray MKV “were both transcoded without significant CPU load,” and that with five concurrent transcodes “the CPU usage only reached about 35%.” The DXP2800 uses the same chip, so it has room for several streams at once from one shared library.
 Mirrored, two drives give you one drive’s worth of space, and a growing 4K library fills that quickly. Memory tops out at 16GB, and there is no path past 2.5GbE. It fits a library that sits comfortably on one large mirrored drive, or a NAS that is mainly a Plex server with backups on the side.

 The N150 version costs $30 more than the DXP4800 Plus, which has the stronger CPU and a 10GbE port, so the N95 version is the one that saves money. Plex’s download page lists TerraMaster packages for TOS 4 through TOS 6, while new units ship with TOS 7, so you may end up running Plex in TerraMaster’s Docker app instead of as a native package.
 The DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus add bays and a faster i5

 For a library that will outgrow four drives, or a household that wants RAID 6 with two-drive protection, the DXP6800 Pro has six bays for $1,099.99, and the DXP8800 Plus has eight bays for $1,369.99. Both use a 10-core Intel Core i5-1235U with Quick Sync and two 10GbE ports. The i5 scores about 40 percent higher than the DXP4800 Plus’s Pentium on PassMark, which helps when Plex shares the box with virtual machines or many Docker apps. Marius Hosting tested the DXP8800 Plus and confirmed that Plex installs with hardware transcoding.
 Both cost more per bay than the DXP4800 Plus, and the six-bay draws more power: Notebookcheck measured the DXP6800 Pro at 37 to 42 watts idle with four hard drives installed. Their Quick Sync media engine is the same Intel generation as the Pentium’s, so the extra money mostly buys bays and CPU rather than transcoding speed.
 The DXP480T Plus has the same i5 and transcodes as well, but it holds only four M.2 SSDs, which top out at 32TB before any RAID protection. Flash costs far more per terabyte than hard drives, so it suits a small server for a modest library rather than a large movie collection.
 Direct play needs no transcoding, and mismatched files do
 When a TV or phone asks Plex for a movie, Plex first tries direct play, which sends the file unchanged. Plex’s direct play guide says that works when the device supports the file’s container, codecs, resolution, and bitrate. A modern smart TV on your home network usually plays H.264 and HEVC files directly, and in that case the NAS does almost no work. Any NAS on this list, including the Synology, can serve a household that only watches that way.
 A phone on cellular data needs a lower bitrate, an older streaming stick may not decode HEVC, and a subtitle format the device cannot draw gets burned into the picture, which Plex says “requires a full transcode of the video stream.” A 4K HDR movie sent to a non-HDR screen needs tone mapping as well, or the colors look washed out. Each of those jobs means decoding the video and re-encoding it in real time.
 A graphics engine with a hardware video encoder does that job with little CPU load, which is also why an Intel mini PC makes a good Plex server . Plex’s hardware-accelerated streaming page says Intel hardware encoding on Linux and Windows has no “artificial limit to the number of simultaneous videos,” and Plex’s tone mapping page lists hardware tone mapping for Intel and NVIDIA. On Linux and NAS systems it needs an Intel chip from the Kaby Lake generation (7th-generation Core) or newer, which every Intel NAS on this list clears.
 Plex charges for hardware transcoding
 Plex Pass costs $6.99 a month or $69.99 a year after the April 2025 price increase, and a lifetime pass rose to $749.99 on July 1, 2026, according to Plex’s announcement . Hardware transcoding needs a pass, and without one Plex transcodes on the CPU even on a NAS with Quick Sync. Since 2025, streaming your own media outside the home also requires Plex Pass or Plex’s cheaper Remote Watch Pass.
 Over three years, the yearly plan adds about $210 to the cost of a Plex server. Jellyfin, a free and open-source media server, does hardware transcoding without a subscription and supports AMD graphics, and it runs in Docker on any of these boxes, including the barebone AOOSTAR units once you install TrueNAS, Unraid, or Linux.
 Close modal 
 AMD-based NAS units are a weaker Plex choice
 Plex added hardware transcoding for AMD graphics on Linux in 2023, but only for SDR video. Plex’s tone mapping documentation has no AMD entry, and its transcoder settings page marks HEVC encoding “(AMD is not supported).” A Plex forum moderator described the state in April 2025 as “only partial HW ( up to HEVC SDR) support for AMD gpus in the transcoder.” In a June 2026 Plex forum report , a Radeon 780M owner reported that hardware encoding failed in the Plex phone apps while it worked in Plex Web, and that rolling back to Plex Media Server 1.42.2 fixed it, which points to a regression in later releases.
 That affects every AMD box with Radeon graphics in the table. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U and WTR MAX and the Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro all have far more CPU than the Intel N100 or Pentium, so their Ryzen cores have more headroom for CPU transcoding. The DXP4800 GT is the exception to that CPU point, with a Ryzen Embedded R2514 that sits between the N100 and the Pentium. The AOOSTAR and Minisforum boxes are better homelab machines for virtual machines and many containers. For Plex, they can transcode SDR video only when the client and driver cooperate, and they cannot tone map HDR on the GPU. If you want one of these boxes, run Jellyfin on it, or keep your library in formats your TVs direct play.
 The Synology DS925+ cannot transcode in hardware
 The DS925+ uses an AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B, a 2018 chip with no integrated graphics. Plex still publishes a package for DSM 7.2.2 and later, so Plex installs and runs, but every transcode lands on four CPU cores that score below an Intel N100. WunderTech’s roundup notes that Synology “moved the DS925+ and DS1525+ to AMD processors with no integrated GPU,” so “hardware transcoding is gone from the current Plus lineup.”
 The DS925+ is still a good backup and photo NAS, with ECC memory and the DSM apps that our UGREEN vs Synology comparison weighs against UGREEN’s, and it can serve Plex to clients that direct play. If you already own one, you can leave the library on it and run Plex on a small Intel mini PC that reads the files over the network.
 A mini PC can do the Plex part instead
 Splitting the work keeps storage on the system you trust for backups and puts transcoding on a cheap, low-power Intel N100 or N150 mini PC. That mini PC reads the library over the network from any NAS, including a Synology or an older box without graphics, and you can replace it later without touching the storage. The cost is two boxes to power and update, so for a new build with no hardware yet, one Intel NAS is simpler. A third option is a mini PC used in place of a NAS , which holds the drives and runs Plex in one box.

 Inclusion requires a manufacturer-verified Intel iGPU (Quick Sync). ARM models and iGPU-less Ryzen models — including current Synology Plus units — are excluded because they cannot hardware-transcode.
 Why Quick Sync decides this purchase
 Plex playback comes in two modes. Direct play hands the file to the client untouched — nearly free for the server, and any NAS can do it. Transcoding re-encodes video on the fly because the client cannot handle the original — a phone on hotel Wi-Fi, a TV that predates HEVC, a burned-in subtitle track — and done in software it saturates a NAS-class CPU with a single 4K stream. Intel's Quick Sync is dedicated silicon that does the same job at a fraction of the load: the modest N100 in a budget UGREEN handles 4K HEVC transcodes that would flatten a far more expensive CPU without an iGPU.
 This is why the brand landscape for Plex looks nothing like the general NAS market. UGREEN's entire Intel lineup qualifies — the value king's Quick Sync coverage is total, from the 2-bay DXP2800 to the 8-bay DXP8800 Plus. QNAP's TS-464 and TS-664 built their reputations on exactly this workload. TerraMaster's Intel boxes qualify at the lowest prices in the table. And Synology — the biggest name in NAS — is absent entirely, because its current Ryzen-based Plus models ship no iGPU. For a transcoding household, the "which brand" debate collapses to the live prices above.
 One licensing note belongs in the budget: Plex gates hardware transcoding behind Plex Pass. Jellyfin, the open-source alternative, uses the same Quick Sync hardware for free and runs on every device in the table. Either way, the hardware you are buying is identical — an Intel iGPU and enough bays for the library.
 Picks by budget and library size
 Starter (2-bay Intel). The UGREEN DXP2800 and TerraMaster F2-425 put real transcoding into mirror-sized boxes. Right for a first server, a single-TV household with remote streaming needs, or a bedroom deployment. The constraint is capacity, not compute — a mirror holds one drive's worth of media, and libraries grow. Buy this tier knowing its ceiling, or skip ahead one.
 Mainstream (4-bay Intel). The center of gravity, and where our best-for-Plex decision card on the hub points: RAID 5 capacity for a serious library plus transcode headroom for a family's worth of simultaneous streams. The QNAP TS-464 is the category's reference box (PCIe for future 10GbE included); UGREEN's 4-bays undercut it with newer silicon; the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro brings an 8-core i3 at a price that reads like a typo. Today's cheapest qualifying 4-bay is the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay at $632.98 .
 Heavy (6-8 bay Intel). Tens of terabytes, multiple 4K remuxes, several concurrent users: UGREEN's DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus pair 10-core i5 chips with dual 10GbE, and QNAP's TS-664 extends the TS platform to RAID 6 territory. At this tier the drives dominate the budget — see the 6-bay and 8-bay guides for the array planning, and the NAS Builder for complete build costs at live prices.
 Sizing the library, honestly
 Media libraries have a one-way ratchet: a 4K remux runs 50-80GB, a Blu-ray rip 25-40GB, a full TV series in 1080p easily 100GB+, and nothing ever gets deleted. A hundred-film collection with a modest TV habit crosses 10TB without trying; enthusiasts cross 50TB with enthusiasm. Work backwards from three years of collecting, add RAID overhead, and you have your drive budget — which is where the real money goes. At today's prices, the cheapest in-stock 20TB drive ( WD , $630.00 ) puts a 60TB-usable RAID 5 library at $2,520.00 in drives alone before the enclosure.
 Drive guidance for this workload is mercifully simple: big CMR drives, nothing exotic. Streaming is sequential reads — the thing spinning drives are best at — so NAS-class or recertified enterprise drives from the live per-terabyte rankings are the right buy, and SSD caching adds little to a workload this linear. Put the flash budget into one more spinning drive instead. The one non-negotiable is CMR over SMR — rebuilds on a media array full of large drives are exactly where SMR's pathological write behavior hurts most.
 Protection strategy differs from a document server, and honestly so: most Plex libraries are re-acquirable, which changes the backup math. RAID 5 or 6 protects the weeks of curation time a rebuild-from-scratch would cost, and that is usually protection enough for the media itself — but the Plex metadata database, watch states and collections are genuinely irreplaceable, tiny, and worth backing up on a schedule to any external target. Protect the library with RAID, protect the curation with backups, and spend the money saved on capacity.
 Network, clients and the first evening
 Plex is kinder to networks than spec-sheet shoppers assume: a 4K remux streams at 40-100Mbps, so gigabit Ethernet carries several simultaneous streams and even good Wi-Fi handles one. The faster ports on these boxes earn their keep during library loading and file management, not playback — which means 2.5GbE is genuinely sufficient for a pure Plex box, and 10GbE is a file-transfer luxury. Wire the NAS to the router if humanly possible; the flakiest Plex setups are almost always Wi-Fi-attached servers, not underpowered ones.
 The first evening's checklist, in order: update the NAS OS and install Plex from the official package source; store the config on the SSD if your model has M.2 (metadata on flash makes browsing snappy even when the library sleeps on spinning drives); point Plex at your media folders with the recommended naming scheme; enable hardware transcoding in Plex settings (it is off by default even on Quick Sync boxes); and set remote access through Plex's relay rather than port-forwarding the NAS itself. Then play the ugliest file you own on the weakest client you own — if that transcode is smooth, everything else will be.
 One honest scope note: this page covers NAS appliances, and a used mini-PC with an Intel chip plus a USB enclosure can undercut all of them for pure transcoding duty. What the NAS buys you is the storage half done properly — RAID, snapshots, drive management, one box instead of a science project. Buyers tempted by the DIY route should price it against the live table above with drives included; the gap is usually smaller than expected, and the appliance keeps weekends free.
 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best NAS for Plex in 2026? For most Plex households: the cheapest in-stock Intel-iGPU 4-bay, currently the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay at $632.98 in our live table. It hardware-transcodes 4K, holds a RAID 5 library, and leaves headroom for growth. Budget setups can start on an Intel 2-bay; heavy libraries step up to the 6- and 8-bay Intel models. Every price above is live.
 Do I really need hardware transcoding for Plex? If every client always direct-plays your exact formats — same codec, container and subtitles the TV supports natively — no. In practice, remote streams, phones, bandwidth limits, burned-in subtitles and older TVs all force transcodes, and one software-transcoded 4K stream will bring a NAS CPU to its knees. A Quick Sync iGPU turns that same transcode into a light workload. Buying transcode capability is buying insurance against how your library actually gets watched.
 Does Plex hardware transcoding require Plex Pass? Yes — hardware-accelerated transcoding is a Plex Pass feature. Factor the subscription (or lifetime pass) into the build budget, or consider Jellyfin, which is free and uses the same Intel Quick Sync hardware. Every iGPU model in our table accelerates both.
 Why are Synology NAS absent from this page? Current Synology Plus models use AMD Ryzen embedded CPUs with no integrated GPU, so they cannot hardware-transcode — they only qualify for direct-play libraries. This page lists devices we have verified as transcode-capable. If you want DSM anyway for a direct-play setup, the Synology brand page covers the lineup with live prices.
 How many drives does a Plex NAS need? Media libraries grow monotonically — nobody deletes movies — so buy bays for the library you will have in three years. A 4-bay in RAID 5 (three drives usable) is the mainstream answer; serious collections go six bays and RAID 6. Spinning drives are the right medium: sequential streaming is what hard drives do best, and per-terabyte pricing crushes SSDs for this workload.
 Can a cheap ARM NAS run Plex at all? It can run the server and direct-play to one or two clients, and for a disciplined single-TV household that genuinely suffices. What it cannot do is transcode meaningfully — one incompatible client turns playback into a slideshow. The price gap between ARM boxes and the cheapest Intel-iGPU models in our live table is modest; for Plex it is the highest-value money in the build.

 The DXP4800 Plus lists at $619.99. Its Pentium Gold 8505 has one performance core and four efficiency cores, scores about 9,000 on PassMark’s CPU test, and includes Intel’s Quick Sync video engine. Plex’s own tone-mapping documentation lists Intel processors from Kaby Lake onward for hardware HDR-to-SDR conversion on Linux and NAS servers, so a 4K HDR movie can play on an older TV or a phone without washed-out colors. Plex needs a Plex Pass subscription for hardware transcoding; Jellyfin does it for free.
 One 10GbE port and one 2.5GbE port come on the board, so a desktop with a 10GbE card can copy files at around 1,100 MB/s once the drive array can keep up. The operating system lives on its own 128GB SSD, which leaves the four bays and two PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots free for data and gives TrueNAS or Unraid a separate drive to install on. Memory starts at 8GB of DDR5 and goes to 64GB across two slots, and there is no drive compatibility list: any SATA drive or NVMe SSD works.
 UGREEN’s software has less depth than Synology’s. Simon Handby at ITPro wrote that “UGOS Pro is extremely user-friendly, and generally quite capable, but it doesn’t have the depth you might expect from, say, Synology Disk Station Manager,” and counted 29 apps in its App Center. Plex installs through Docker rather than as a one-click package. Under a long, heavy load, KitGuru saw the CPU reach 100 degrees Celsius and the fan get loud, and measured about 24 watts at idle with four hard drives installed. The memory UGREEN labels “ODECC” is the on-die error correction built into every DDR5 chip, not ECC memory modules.
 UGREEN DXP4800 GT adds a second 10GbE port and ECC memory support
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 GT
 Versatile 
 4-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 
 List price $659.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The DXP4800 GT launched in June 2026 and lists at $659.99, $40 more than the DXP4800 Plus. For that money it has two 10GbE ports, an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 that accepts ECC memory modules, and two bays that also take U.2 NVMe SSDs. Alastair Jennings at TechRadar edited video straight off it over 10GbE and called it “the best-value 4-bay NAS with 10GbE networking that I have seen yet.” PCWorld gave it an Editors’ Choice award and measured 25 watts at idle with the drives asleep and 40 to 42 watts in normal use.
 The Radeon Vega graphics transcode H.264 and H.265 for Plex, but Lon.TV’s tests of AMD’s Vega-based chips found that “hardware tone mapping is not supported on these chips,” so HDR movies look washed out when Plex converts them (Lon.TV did not test the R2514 itself). The 8GB memory module in the box is not ECC, so you have to buy ECC modules to get the protection, and a single module runs in single-channel mode. The OS sits on a 64GB eMMC chip soldered to the board, which makes a TrueNAS or Unraid install less straightforward than on the DXP4800 Plus. The two M.2 slots also run at PCIe 3.0 x2, about 2GB/s per SSD, against PCIe 4.0 on the DXP4800 Plus.
 Those limits matter less when your library is mostly SDR video or your TVs play HDR files directly, and in that case the GT’s second 10GbE port and ECC support are worth the extra $40 at list price. It is also the only box here that can link two machines at full 10GbE speed at once without a switch.
 Synology DS925+ has the strongest backup software
 Synology DiskStation DS925+
 Best for Backups 
 4-Bay 2.5GbE 4GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B 
 List price $700.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The DS925+ runs DSM, Synology’s operating system. Its Hyper Backup app makes versioned, encrypted backups of the NAS to a USB drive, another NAS, or cloud storage. Active Backup for Business backs up Windows and Mac computers to the NAS, and Active Backup for Microsoft 365 does the same for Microsoft 365 accounts, both with no per-seat fee. Synology Photos, Synology Drive, and Snapshot Replication have years of fixes behind them. For a home or small office that wants a backup appliance and does not want to maintain Docker containers, none of the other four boxes ships with a comparable backup suite.
 Its chip is the oldest of the five, and its network ports tie the WTR Pro’s as the slowest. The Ryzen V1500B has no graphics engine, so Plex and Jellyfin transcode on its four CPU cores, which are too slow for 4K HEVC. The two 2.5GbE ports are the network ceiling for the life of the box, because it has no PCIe slot or network upgrade slot. Memory starts at 4GB of ECC DDR4 and tops out at 32GB. Dong Knows Tech found that “Its network throughput is generally limited by the 2.5Gbps ports,” and measured about 730 watt-hours per day with four hard drives, an average of about 30 watts.
 Drive support is better than at launch. Synology’s DSM 7.3 release in October 2025 restored storage-pool creation with third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, so WD Red and Seagate IronWolf drives work in the four bays. The two M.2 slots still take only Synology-listed NVMe SSDs for new pools and caches, per Synology’s drive compatibility policy . Synology’s cheaper four-bay, the DS425+ , uses a Celeron J4125 from 2019 with 2GB of memory; that is a step down from the DS925+ in both CPU and memory. Our UGREEN vs Synology comparison covers the software gap in more detail.
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus has 5GbE and a cheaper N95 version
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 Budget Pick 
 4-Bay 5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N95 
 List price $599.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The F4-425 Plus comes in two versions in the same aluminum case. The N150 model lists at $649.99 with 16GB of DDR5, and the N95 model lists at $599.99 with 8GB of DDR4. Both have two 5GbE ports, three M.2 NVMe slots, and Intel Quick Sync for Plex and Jellyfin, and both run TerraMaster’s TOS 7 or a third-party system such as Unraid. TOS includes TRAID, which mixes drive sizes in one array the way Synology’s SHR does.
 A 5GbE port carries about 500 to 550 MB/s, roughly double a 2.5GbE port, and it falls back to 2.5GbE or 1GbE on an older switch. The limits are the M.2 slots, which get one PCIe 3.0 lane each and top out just under 1,000 MB/s, the single memory slot, and the lack of a PCIe slot. Mark Pickavance at TechRadar wrote that “A few niggles, like the feet that fall off, suggest this product was rushed to market,” while Rob Andrews at NASCompares measured about 13 watts at idle with three SSDs and no hard drives.
 At list price the N150 model costs $30 more than the DXP4800 Plus, which has a faster CPU and a 10GbE port, so the N150 version is mostly a sale-price buy. The N95 model lists $20 below the DXP4800 Plus. The N95 model at $599.99 is the cheapest box here that ships with its own NAS software, though running more than a few containers on it calls for a memory upgrade.
 AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U has the fastest CPU and no software
 AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U
 Best Performance 
 4-Bay 2.5GbE No RAM AMD Ryzen 7 5825U 
 List price $379.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The WTR Pro 5825U is a barebone four-bay box with an eight-core, 16-thread Ryzen 7 5825U, a laptop chip from 2022 with a PassMark score of about 17,774, double the DXP4800 Plus. It lists at $379.00 with no memory, no SSD, and no NAS software. Add two DDR4 SO-DIMMs and an NVMe drive for the operating system, then install TrueNAS, Unraid, Proxmox, or a Linux distribution yourself. In return you get enough CPU for several virtual machines and containers at once, two M.2 slots at PCIe 3.0 x4, and two 2.5GbE ports.
 The drive bays are not hot-swappable, so you have to power down to replace a failed drive, and Rob Andrews at NASCompares found the trays hard to use: “Trying to get a hard drive out of these trays is incredibly difficult.” Andrews measured 31 to 32 dBA at idle with four drives, and NotebookCheck measured 37 to 38 dB(A) at idle with no hard drives installed. There is no vendor app store, phone backup app, or remote-access service, and 10GbE means adding a USB adapter or giving up an M.2 slot to a network card.
 Close modal 
 Network speed limits file copies more than the CPU does
 A 2.5GbE port moves about 280 MB/s in practice. That is enough to stream any video file, back up phones, and serve a family’s documents, and it is about as fast as a single hard drive. Four hard drives in RAID 5 can read faster than that, so a 2.5GbE port becomes the bottleneck the moment you copy a large folder of photos or video from a desktop. A 10GbE port raises the ceiling to about 1,100 MB/s, and 5GbE sits in between.
 Faster ports only help if the rest of the path matches. A 10GbE NAS needs a 10GbE card or adapter in the computer and either a 10GbE switch or a direct cable between the two. If your router and switch are gigabit, every box here runs at about 110 MB/s until you upgrade them. Our article on 10GbE versus 2.5GbE for a home NAS works through when the upgrade pays off. The DS925+ has no way to add a faster port later, and the WTR Pro has no built-in route to 10GbE short of a USB adapter or an M.2 network card that gives up an SSD slot, while the two UGREEN boxes have 10GbE built in.
 RAID 5 or RAID 6 on four drives
 With four drives, RAID 5 gives you three drives of usable space and survives one failure. RAID 6 gives you two drives of usable space and survives two failures. The case for RAID 6 is the rebuild: when a drive fails, the NAS has to read every sector of the other three to rebuild the fourth, which can take a day or more on large drives, and a second failure during that window loses the array in RAID 5. NASCompares’ guide treats RAID 5 as reasonable for small arrays and leans toward RAID 6 as drives grow.
 For a typical home NAS with four drives of 8TB to 16TB, RAID 5 plus a separate backup is a reasonable choice, and RAID 6 is the safer one if you can give up the space. Either way, RAID is not a backup. It keeps the NAS running after a drive dies; it does nothing about a deleted folder, ransomware, a failed power supply, or a fire. Keep a second copy of anything you care about on a USB drive, another NAS, or cloud storage.

 If four bays already looks tight, the Minisforum N5 Air is a five-bay box that lists at $535.00 barebone, with an eight-core Ryzen 7 255, 10GbE plus 5GbE, and a PCIe slot. The UGREEN DXP480T Plus goes the other way, with four M.2 slots and no drive bays, for silent all-flash storage .  Rules for Choosing a 4 -Bay NAS
 1 Start with 3 equal drives under SHR / RAID 5 to enjoy 1-drive parity while leaving 1 bay free for zero-downtime future expansion. 
 2 Use RAID 5 for media and backups to maximize capacity (75% usable). Choose RAID 6 / SHR-2 dual parity for irreplaceable business files. 
 3 If streaming 4K movies with subtitle transcoding, verify that the NAS processor features an Intel Quick Sync GPU. 
 4 Pair 4-bay systems with a compatible UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) to prevent array corruption during unexpected power outages. 
 Mistakes to Avoid Before Buying
 ✕ Filling all 4 bays on day 1 with small 2TB drives, eliminating easy expansion. 
 ✕ Choosing a non-iGPU processor (like AMD Ryzen V1500B) when intensive 4K Plex hardware transcoding is required. 
 ✕ Overlooking noise: 4 × 7200rpm drives can be audible in a bedroom; locate the NAS in an office or utility closet. 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Why is a 4-bay NAS considered the best choice for home use?
 A 4-bay NAS hits the mathematical sweet spot: RAID 5 gives you 75% usable capacity (versus 50% in a 2-bay RAID 1 mirror), while providing full 1-disk failure protection. You can also populate 3 bays initially and preserve the 4th bay for hassle-free storage expansion.
 What is the cheapest 4-bay NAS in 2026?
 Enclosures like the TerraMaster F4-424 and UGREEN DXP4800 represent the most affordable modern 4-bay entry points with Intel processors, starting around $400 to $450 before hard drives.
 How much does a complete 4-bay NAS cost with hard drives?
 Use the exact-model cost table below the picks and compare both total spend and protected capacity. Three 12TB drives under single parity provide 24TB decimal capacity; four provide 36TB. Checkout prices, tax, shipping, backup storage, and network upgrades can change the final budget.
 Can I start a 4-bay NAS with just 2 hard drives?
 Some systems allow a two-drive mirror or SHR pool to grow by adding disks and migrating to single parity. The supported steps depend on the operating system and existing RAID layout; conversion is not automatic on every NAS. Read the model-specific procedure and verify your independent backup before changing the pool.
 What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6 in a 4-bay NAS?
 RAID 5 allocates one drive worth of storage to parity (75% usable with 4 drives) and survives one disk failure. RAID 6 uses dual parity (50% usable with 4 drives) and survives two simultaneous drive crashes, which is recommended for mission-critical business retention or when rebuilding high-capacity 16TB+ arrays.

 Bottom line 
 Buy a four-bay NAS for a home, since it leaves room for RAID and bigger drives later. Pick the software first, then the hardware. RAID is not a backup, so keep a second copy of your files somewhere else.
Recommendation
 Buy the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus for Plex, Docker, and fast transfers. Buy the Synology DS925+ if backups matter most.
 How to use the NAS comparison chart
 Click a column heading to sort by it, and click it again to reverse the order. The chips above the table narrow the list by bay count (2-bay, 4-bay, or 5 or more) and by four features: 10GbE networking, ECC memory, hardware transcoding, and all-flash designs . The feature chips stack, so ticking 10GbE and ECC together shows only models that have both. Tick Compare on two to four rows to see their full specs side by side. Each model name opens its product page, with the full spec sheet, what reviewers found, and current prices.
 Some models come in more than one configuration, such as a barebone unit and versions with memory installed. Each configuration gets its own row, and the processor and installed memory show under the model name. Every model in the chart ships without drives, so no price here includes storage. Budget for drives separately; the cost section below shows how quickly they add up.
 What each column means
 Bays counts the 3.5-inch drive bays, which also take 2.5-inch drives. A model marked all-flash has no hard drive bays and holds only M.2 SSDs. M.2 is the number of M.2 NVMe slots free for your own SSDs. On most models these slots work as an SSD cache or as a separate storage pool. A slot that the maker fills with the system drive does not count.
 Max LAN is the fastest built-in Ethernet port. Some models add a second, slower port, and the chart lists only the faster one. Filter for 10GbE if you plan to move large files across a 10GbE network.
 ECC reads Yes only when the NAS supports ECC SO-DIMM memory modules. These modules carry extra check bits, so the processor can detect and correct memory errors, whether they happen inside a memory chip or on the way to the processor. DDR5 memory also has on-die ECC, which corrects errors only inside each memory chip, so the chart counts on-die ECC as No.
 Transcode reads Yes when the processor has a graphics engine that converts video in hardware. Media servers use it to stream to phones, TVs, and browsers that cannot play the original file. Jellyfin uses it on every model marked Yes; Plex support depends on the chip, as the transcoding section below explains. The Synology DS925+ reads No because its AMD Ryzen V1500B has no graphics engine.
 Idle is the power draw in watts with the NAS switched on and doing no work, as measured by the maker or a reviewer. The test conditions vary by source. Some figures have the hard drives spun down, some have no drives installed, and some have drives spinning. Synology measured the DS925+ at 12.33 W with four hard drives in hibernation, while the DXP6800 Pro figure of 22.4 W comes from a unit with no drives at all. Compare idle figures only when the conditions match, and check each product page for the conditions behind its number.
 RAM Max is the most memory the unit supports. Price starts as the list price for that configuration, marked MSRP. When a current retailer price is available, the chart shows it instead, with the date and time it was checked, and Buying options lists each store.
 Who needs a NAS
 A NAS (network-attached storage) is a small computer built to hold hard drives and share them over your home network. Every phone, laptop, TV, and streaming box on the network can reach the same files, and the NAS keeps running when your computers are off. The common jobs are phone photo backup, a backup target for Windows and Mac computers, a shared family drive, and a media library for Plex or Jellyfin. Newer models with faster chips also run Docker containers such as Home Assistant or Pi-hole, and a few virtual machines.
 You probably need one if your photos and documents live on a single laptop or a single USB drive, if two or more people need the same files, or if your media library has outgrown what a streaming box can hold. You probably do not need one if everything you care about already fits in a cloud plan you pay for and you have no media library. A NAS is also not the right tool for someone who wants no maintenance at all: every model in the chart needs updates, drive health checks, and a backup of its own.
 A NAS, a mini PC home server, or cloud storage
 Cloud storage is the simplest option. Google, Apple, and Microsoft keep the copies, handle the hardware, and give you access anywhere. The costs are a monthly fee that grows with your library, a copy of your files on someone else’s servers, and download speeds limited by your internet connection. Cloud storage also works as the off-site second copy for a NAS.
 A mini PC can do much of what a NAS does. It runs the same Linux, Docker, and Plex software, and it often has a faster processor for the money. It has little room for drives. A typical mini PC takes one or two M.2 SSDs and no 3.5-inch hard drives, so large libraries end up on USB enclosures. Our guides to using a mini PC as a NAS and building a mini PC home server cover that route.
 A NAS sits between the two. It holds two to eight hard drives, usually in hot-swap trays, protects them with RAID, and comes with software that handles sharing, backup, and photo sync without a Linux command line. Hard drives cost far less per terabyte than SSDs, so a NAS is the cheapest way to keep tens of terabytes at home. Several NAS models in the chart also have processors as fast as a mid-range mini PC, so one box can do both jobs.
 What a NAS operating system does
 The operating system decides more about daily life with a NAS than the hardware does. It sets which RAID types you can use, how backups work, which phone apps you get, and how long the box keeps receiving security fixes. Pick the software you want first, then find hardware that runs it.
 DSM, UGOS Pro, TOS, and MinisCloud OS
 Synology’s DSM runs only on Synology hardware and is the most complete NAS system in the chart. Its backup apps are the main reason to buy Synology: Hyper Backup makes versioned backups to another NAS, a USB drive, or cloud storage, and Active Backup for Business backs up Windows and Mac computers to the NAS. Synology Photos and Synology Drive cover phone photo backup and file sync. Our UGREEN vs Synology comparison goes through those apps in detail.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro runs on every NASync model. It is based on Debian and covers file sharing, a photo app with face and object recognition, file sync, Docker, and virtual machines. Its backup tools are thinner than Synology’s. TerraMaster’s TOS 7 includes TRAID (TerraMaster’s flexible RAID), Btrfs snapshots, a photo app, Docker with Portainer, and backup tools, but no built-in media center app. Minisforum’s MinisCloud OS is the newest of the four; ServeTheHome, Jim’s Garage, and Britec09 all called it unfinished in their N5 Pro reviews, and the first setup runs through a desktop or phone app rather than a web page.
 The DS925+ and the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus install their systems on the data drives. UGREEN puts UGOS Pro on its own eMMC chip or SSD (32GB of eMMC on the DXP2800, 64GB on the DXP4800 GT, and a 128GB SSD on the larger models), and the Minisforum units ship with a small system SSD in one of their M.2 slots. A separate system drive makes it easier to replace the operating system without touching your data.
 Synology’s drive rules
 Synology is the only maker in the chart with a drive compatibility list that decides what you can install. When the DS925+ launched in 2025, it would not install DSM on hard drives outside that list. Synology reversed course with DSM 7.3 on October 8, 2025 , and 2025 DiskStation Plus models now accept third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs for new storage pools.
 The M.2 slots are still restricted. Synology’s drive compatibility policy lists unlisted M.2 NVMe SSDs in DS Plus models as supported only when migrated from an older Synology system, not for new pools or caches. On a DS925+, that means Synology’s own NVMe SSDs if you want to use the M.2 slots at all. UGREEN, TerraMaster, Minisforum, and AOOSTAR have no drive list you have to follow.
 TrueNAS, Unraid, and Proxmox on NAS hardware
 Every model in the chart except the DS925+ is an x86 PC with drive bays that accepts a third-party system. TrueNAS Community Edition is free, runs on Debian, and is built on OpenZFS, with Docker apps and virtual machines. Unraid is a paid system that lets you mix drives of different sizes in one array and add drives one at a time. Proxmox is a virtual machine host, and some owners run TrueNAS inside a Proxmox virtual machine; Jim’s Garage set up the Minisforum N5 Pro that way.
 UGREEN allows third-party systems and keeps the hardware warranty, though it does not support the software, and on the DXP2800 and DXP8800 Plus you must disable a watchdog timer in the BIOS first. The 64GB eMMC system drive on the DXP4800 GT makes other installs less direct than on the UGREEN models with a system SSD. Minisforum supports Windows 11 and Linux on the N5 Air, and reviewers ran Windows 11, Proxmox, and TrueNAS on the N5 Pro. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U ships with no NAS system at all, so you bring your own from the start. The common snag across all of them is fan control: under TrueNAS or Unraid, the fans may run too fast or too slow until you set them up.
 A third-party system also protects you against the end of vendor updates. If the maker stops updating a model, TrueNAS or Unraid keeps running on standard x86 hardware. A Synology box runs DSM and nothing else in any supported way.
 Apps, Docker, and virtual machines
 Docker containers are small, self-contained apps: Home Assistant, Pi-hole, Immich for photos, a password manager, a download client. Every system in the chart runs them, and they need little processor power, but each one takes memory. A handful of containers fits comfortably in 8GB. The DS925+ ships with 4GB, which fills quickly once you add containers.
 Virtual machines are full operating systems running inside the NAS, such as a Windows desktop or a Linux test server. They need processor cores and several gigabytes of memory each. The DS925+, with four cores and 4GB installed, suits one small virtual machine at most. The Core i5 UGREEN models (10 cores), the AOOSTAR and the Minisforum N5 Air (6 or 8 cores), and the N5 Pro (12 cores) have room for several.
 NAS hardware
 Drive bays and capacity
 Bays set how much storage the NAS can hold and which RAID types it can use. Two bays give you a mirror: two drives with the same data, so one can fail. Four bays allow RAID 5, where one drive’s worth of space holds parity and the rest holds data, so four 12TB drives give about 36TB of usable space. RAID 6 survives two failed drives at the cost of two drives of space; it needs at least four drives but makes more sense with five or more, since four-drive RAID 6 leaves only half the raw space.
 For most homes, four bays are the practical minimum. A two-bay box such as the UGREEN DXP2800 costs less, but a mirror gives you only half the raw capacity, and to grow it you must replace both drives. Four bays let you start with three drives and add a fourth later. The chart has four-bay models from UGREEN, Synology, TerraMaster, and AOOSTAR, five-bay models from Minisforum, and six- and eight-bay models from UGREEN.
 Look at hot-swap trays too. Most models in the chart let you pull a failed drive while the NAS is running. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U does not, so you must shut it down to change a drive. The UGREEN DXP480T Plus has no drive bays at all: it holds four M.2 SSDs for up to 32TB of flash storage in a box about the size of a Mac mini.
 RAID, file systems, and why RAID is not a backup
 RAID keeps the NAS running when a drive fails. It does not protect you from deleting a file, from ransomware that encrypts your shares, from a power surge that kills every drive, or from a fire. Synology states it plainly in its knowledge base: “ RAID (classic and SHR) is not a backup solution .” The TrueNAS ZFS primer says the same: “RAID and disk redundancy are not substitutes for a reliable backup strategy.” The usual rule is 3-2-1 : three copies of your data, on two different media, with one copy off-site. For a NAS, that means a second copy on a USB drive or another NAS, and a third in cloud storage or at another house.
 Classic RAID 5 treats every drive as the size of the smallest one. Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR) combines drives of different sizes to use more of the space, and needs at least four drives for SHR-2, which survives two failures. TerraMaster’s TRAID works on the same idea. Unraid keeps a separate file system on each data drive and protects them with one or two parity drives, and Unraid’s documentation says the parity drive must be at least as large as the largest data drive. UGOS Pro offers standard RAID levels. MinisCloud OS builds only ZFS pools, so its choices are ZFS layouts: a stripe, a mirror, RAIDZ1 (similar to RAID 5), and RAIDZ2 (similar to RAID 6), which Minisforum lists as RAID 0, 1, 5, and 6.
 DSM, UGOS Pro, and TOS offer Btrfs, which supports snapshots: saved versions of a folder that you can roll back to after an accidental deletion or a ransomware attack, as long as the attack does not reach the snapshots themselves. They also offer ext4, which is simpler and has no snapshots. TrueNAS uses ZFS, which checksums every block it writes. When it finds a block that does not match its checksum on a mirrored or RAIDZ pool, it replaces the bad data with a good copy. DSM, UGOS Pro, and TOS do not use ZFS. MinisCloud OS on the Minisforum units uses ZFS only, with no Btrfs or ext4. On the other models you get ZFS by installing TrueNAS or a Linux distribution that supports it.
 CMR and SMR hard drives
 Buy NAS drives that use CMR (conventional magnetic recording). Some cheaper drives use SMR (shingled magnetic recording), which overlaps data tracks to fit more on a platter and slows down badly during long writes such as a RAID rebuild. Western Digital says on its blog that WD Red Plus is the name for its CMR NAS drives from 1TB to 14TB, while its 2TB to 6TB WD Red drives use device-managed SMR. TrueNAS found that one WD Red SMR model can enter a faulty state under heavy writes, including rebuilds, and recommends CMR drives.
 WD Red Plus, WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf, and Seagate IronWolf Pro are the common NAS lines, and each maker’s product page states the recording type. Check it before you buy, especially for drives of 6TB or less.
 M.2 slots for cache or a storage pool
 Most models in the chart have two or more M.2 NVMe slots. As a cache, the SSDs hold copies of files you open often so the NAS can serve them faster than the hard drives. As a separate storage pool, the SSDs become their own fast volume, which suits Docker apps and their databases. With apps on SSDs, the hard drives can spin down when nobody is using them, which saves power and noise.
 The lane count on each slot sets its top speed. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus gives each of its three M.2 slots one PCIe 3.0 lane, so one drive tops out just under 1,000 MB/s. The Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro run their free slots at x2 and x1, and the UGREEN DXP4800 GT at PCIe 3.0 x2. The DXP480T Plus runs two of its four slots at PCIe 4.0 x4. On most models the network is the slower link anyway, since a 2.5GbE port moves about 300 MB/s and a 10GbE port about 1,100 MB/s.
 Check what the M.2 slots accept before you count on them. On the DS925+, they take only Synology’s SSDs. On the AOOSTAR, which ships barebone, one of the two slots usually holds the operating system drive, which leaves one for data. The DXP480T Plus and DXP4800 Plus have no room for SSDs with their own full-height heatsinks.
 U.2 bays
 U.2 is a connector for data-center NVMe SSDs, which come in a 2.5-inch drive shape and reach larger capacities than M.2 drives. Two models in the chart accept them. On the UGREEN DXP4800 GT , bays 1 and 2 take a U.2 drive in place of a SATA drive, on a PCIe 3.0 x4 link. The Minisforum N5 Pro takes two U.2 drives through an included adapter in its data M.2 slots, limited to 7mm drives of up to 15TB, and the adapter replaces an internal fan. U.2 drives are enterprise SSDs, so this feature suits homelab owners who already have them.
 Processors
 The processor sets how many apps, containers, and virtual machines the NAS can run at once. File sharing and backups need very little. PassMark’s CPU Mark, a multi-thread benchmark score, gives a rough scale for the chips in the chart:
 Processor Cores / threads CPU Mark Models 
 AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B 4 / 8 about 4,500 Synology DS925+ 
 Intel N95, N100, N150 4 / 4 about 5,300 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus, UGREEN DXP2800 
 AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 4 / 8 about 6,700 UGREEN DXP4800 GT 
 Intel Pentium Gold 8505 5 / 6 about 9,000 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus 
 Intel Core i5-1235U 10 / 12 about 12,500 UGREEN DXP480T Plus, DXP6800 Pro, DXP8800 Plus 
 AMD Ryzen 7 5825U 8 / 16 about 17,800 AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U 
 AMD Ryzen 5 7640HS, Ryzen 7 255 6 / 12, 8 / 16 about 23,100 and 28,700 Minisforum N5 Air 
 AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370 12 / 24 about 33,300 Minisforum N5 Pro 
 The Intel N-series chips (N95, N100, N150) are low-power four-core parts that handle file serving, photo backup, Plex with hardware transcoding, and a handful of containers. The Pentium Gold 8505 and Core i5-1235U are laptop chips with more cores and the same Intel graphics engine. The V1500B in the DS925+ belongs to an AMD embedded family that launched in 2018. The laptop-class Ryzen chips in the AOOSTAR and the Minisforum units are several times faster than the N-series and suit owners who want the NAS to be their main home server.
 More processor means more power at full load, but not always at idle. If the NAS will serve files and nothing else, a fast chip is money spent on headroom you will not use. If it will run Plex, a dozen containers, and a Windows virtual machine, the extra cores save you from buying a second computer.
 Hardware transcoding for Plex and Jellyfin
 When Plex or Jellyfin streams a movie to a device that cannot play its format, or to a phone on a slow connection, the server converts the video on the fly. A chip with a built-in video engine does this with little effort. A chip without one does it on the processor cores, and a four-core embedded chip cannot keep up with a 4K HEVC file. If most of your viewing is on a modern TV that plays your files as they are (direct play), transcoding rarely happens and this matters less.
 Every model in the chart except the Synology DS925+ has a video engine. The Intel models use Quick Sync. The AMD models use AMD’s video engine in their Radeon graphics; PCWorld confirmed that the Radeon Vega graphics in the DXP4800 GT transcode H.264 and H.265 in UGREEN’s own video app. Plex’s hardware acceleration article says the feature “requires an active Plex Pass subscription,” and its Linux instructions cover Intel graphics and NVIDIA cards but do not list AMD graphics. Jellyfin is free, and its documentation covers Intel Quick Sync and AMD graphics through VA-API on Linux. Plex on AMD graphics is less certain. Lon.TV tested Plex under Unraid on four AMD mini PCs: hardware transcoding worked on the Zen 2 and Zen 3 chips with Vega graphics, but “hardware tone mapping is not supported on these chips,” so HDR video looked washed out, and on the Zen 4 and Zen 5 chips “hardware transcoding does not work.” The AOOSTAR’s Ryzen 7 5825U and the DXP4800 GT’s R2514 also use Vega graphics; Lon.TV did not test these two chips, but expect the same result, with Plex transcoding and no HDR tone mapping. The Minisforum N5 Air (Zen 4) and N5 Pro (Zen 5) use the same generations that failed; Lon.TV tested a Ryzen AI 365, not these exact chips. Plex runs on those two, but it transcodes on the processor cores. If Plex is the main job, an Intel model is the safer choice; our guide to setting up a Plex server on a mini PC covers Quick Sync in more detail.
 Memory and ECC
 Memory holds the operating system, the file cache, and every app you run. For a NAS that stores files and backs up phones, 4GB to 8GB is enough. Docker containers and virtual machines each take more, and ZFS uses spare memory as a read cache, so a TrueNAS build does better with more memory. Most models ship with 8GB, the DS925+ ships with 4GB, and the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N150 model ships with 16GB. The AOOSTAR and the barebone Minisforum configurations ship with none, so add the cost of memory to their prices.
 ECC (error-correcting code) memory detects and fixes memory errors before bad data reaches your drives. It needs support from the processor and the motherboard as well as ECC modules. Three models in the chart support it: the Synology DS925+, which ships with a 4GB ECC module; the UGREEN DXP4800 GT, which supports ECC modules but ships with a standard non-ECC module, so you have to buy ECC memory to get the protection; and the Minisforum N5 Pro, which takes ECC or non-ECC DDR5 and sells configurations with 48GB or 96GB of ECC installed.
 Spec sheets for many DDR5 models list “on-die ECC” or “ODECC.” Every DDR5 chip has this. It corrects errors inside each memory chip but does not check data on its way between the memory and the processor, which is the part ECC modules protect. The chart counts on-die ECC as No for that reason. ECC is worth having on a box that holds the only copy of irreplaceable files, but it does not replace a backup, and it matters less than drive redundancy and a second copy of your data.
 The DXP2800 and the TerraMaster have one memory slot each, which caps the DXP2800 at 16GB and the F4-425 Plus N150 model at 32GB. Models with two slots run in dual channel once both are filled, which gives the processor more memory bandwidth. Synology asks for matched pairs and recommends its own modules for the DS925+.
 2.5GbE, 5GbE, and 10GbE networking
 A 2.5GbE port carries at most 312 MB/s before network overhead, and a little less in practice. A single large NAS hard drive reads at a similar speed; Seagate rates its 24TB IronWolf Pro at 240 MB/s sustained. A four-drive RAID array reading in parallel, or any NVMe SSD, is faster than 2.5GbE can carry. A 5GbE port raises the limit to 625 MB/s before overhead (NASCompares measured about 470 MB/s reads over one 5GbE link on the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus with an SSD cache), and a 10GbE port to about 1,100 MB/s in practice.
 Network speed matters for copying large files: video projects, full-computer backups, and restores. It matters little for streaming video, phone photo backup, or Docker apps, which stay far below 2.5GbE. The DS925+, the AOOSTAR, and the DXP2800 top out at 2.5GbE. The TerraMaster has two 5GbE ports. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus has one 10GbE and one 2.5GbE port, the DXP480T Plus has one 10GbE port, the DXP4800 GT, DXP6800 Pro, and DXP8800 Plus have two, and the Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro pair 10GbE with 5GbE.
 A fast port on the NAS helps only if the rest of the path matches. Your router or switch needs a port at the same speed, and the computer on the other end needs a matching network adapter. If the router has only 1GbE ports, a 10GbE NAS behind it moves files at a little over 100 MB/s, and a laptop without an Ethernet port needs a USB or Thunderbolt adapter. You can connect one computer straight to the NAS with a cable and skip the switch. Our article on 10GbE versus 2.5GbE for a home NAS works through when the upgrade pays off.
 Two ports at the same speed can also be combined with link aggregation for failover or for more total bandwidth across several computers. Aggregation does not make one file copy to one computer faster.
 PCIe slots and expansion units
 A PCIe slot lets you add a faster network card, an SFP+ card for fiber or direct-attach cables, or an NVMe adapter. Four models in the chart have one: the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus (PCIe 4.0 x4, low-profile, and you have to take the case apart to reach it) and the Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro (an x16-size slot for low-profile cards, wired at PCIe 4.0 x4). The Minisforum units also have an OCuLink port, which can connect an external graphics card.
 The DS925+ has no PCIe slot and no network upgrade slot, so it stays at 2.5GbE for life. It does support Synology’s DX525 expansion unit, which adds five bays over a USB-C link at 5Gbps, for nine bays in total. The drives in the expansion unit share that link. None of the other models in the chart supports an expansion unit, so buy enough bays up front.
 Power draw and noise
 A NAS runs around the clock, so idle power matters more than peak power. The measured idle figures behind the chart range from about 5 W for the DXP2800 with one drive asleep (UGREEN’s lab figure) to 45 to 49 W for the Minisforum N5 Pro with five 28TB hard drives installed ( ServeTheHome’s measurement ). The test conditions explain most of that range. Hard drives add a large share: Seagate’s 24TB IronWolf Pro draws 6.7 W at idle and 1.2 W asleep, so four spinning drives add about 27 W on their own. Dong Knows Tech measured about 730 watt-hours a day from the DS925+ with four hard drives, an average of about 30 W.
 At 30 W around the clock, a NAS uses about 263 kilowatt-hours a year, which comes to about $45 at 17 cents per kilowatt-hour. Our breakdown of what a server costs to run 24/7 has the math for other rates. To lower the bill, let the drives spin down when idle, put apps on an M.2 pool so the hard drives can sleep, and pick a chip no bigger than your workload.
 The drives also make most of the noise. Synology rates the DS925+ at 20.5 dB(A) at idle with its own drives, while NASCompares measured 36 to 37 dB(A) fully idle in its review. Seagate rates the 24TB IronWolf Pro at 28 dB(A) idle and 32 dB(A) while seeking, per drive. Large 7,200 rpm drives click and hum in a quiet room no matter which box they sit in. If the NAS will live in a bedroom or living room, plan for a closet, a basement, or smaller, quieter drives. The all-flash DXP480T Plus runs under 30 dB at idle in Liliputing’s test , but its fans are audible during large copies.
 USB, Thunderbolt, and HDMI
 Every model has USB ports for backing up to an external drive or importing files from a camera card reader. Most have 10Gbps USB-A or USB-C ports, which are fast enough for an external hard drive or SSD. The DS925+ has two 5Gbps USB-A ports, and its USB-C port connects only to the DX525.
 Three UGREEN models have two Thunderbolt 4 ports: the DXP480T Plus, DXP6800 Pro, and DXP8800 Plus. Thunderbolt lets a Mac or PC connect straight to the NAS at up to 40Gb/s without a 10GbE switch, which suits a video editor working from one desk. One DXP6800 Pro owner could not get the Thunderbolt link to work with a Mac, so keep 10GbE as a second fast path. The Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro have two USB4 ports each.
 Most models also have an HDMI port. On the TerraMaster, HDMI gives only a text terminal. Under a third-party system such as Proxmox or Windows, it works as a normal display output for setup and troubleshooting.
 Diskless prices and the cost of drives
 Every NAS in the chart ships without drives, and the drives often cost as much as the NAS or more. Before comparing box prices, add the drives you need to reach your target capacity, plus a spare drive or a backup drive. For four-bay models, list prices run from $379 for the barebone AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U to $700 for the Synology DS925+, with the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at $619.99, the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N150 model at $649.99, and the UGREEN DXP4800 GT at $659.99. The five-bay Minisforum N5 Air lists from $495 barebone, the N5 Pro from $899 barebone, and the six- and eight-bay UGREEN models at $1,099.99 and $1,369.99. The two-bay DXP2800 lists at $389.99.
 Barebone units need more than drives. The AOOSTAR ships with no memory, no system drive, and no NAS software, so add memory and an M.2 SSD for the operating system. The barebone Minisforum configurations include a system SSD but no memory. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N150 model ships with 16GB, twice the 8GB in UGREEN’s four-bay models, and its N95 model with 8GB lists at $599.99.
 Drive prices change often, so the chart does not include them. Compare drives by price per terabyte, which varies by capacity; the largest size is not always the cheapest per terabyte. Fewer, larger drives leave bays free for later and use less power than a full set of small drives, since each spinning drive adds several watts.
 Which NAS fits which buyer
 For a home that wants Plex or Jellyfin, Docker apps, and fast file transfers in one box, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the default four-bay pick. It has a 10GbE port, Quick Sync for transcoding, M.2 slots that take any SSD, and a system SSD that makes TrueNAS an easy install later. Its limits are UGOS Pro’s thinner backup tools and no ECC modules. If you want ECC and dual 10GbE in four bays, the DXP4800 GT adds both, plus U.2 support, for a lower list price, but you must buy ECC memory separately.
 For backup first, pick the Synology DS925+ . DSM’s backup apps, ECC memory, and the DX525 expansion option suit a home or small office that wants the NAS to protect computers and photos with little attention. Accept its limits before you buy: 2.5GbE for life, no hardware transcoding, only 4GB of memory installed, and M.2 slots locked to Synology SSDs. Our UGREEN vs Synology comparison sets these two side by side.
 For a first NAS with faster ports than 2.5GbE, the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus pairs four bays with an Intel N150, 16GB of memory, three M.2 slots, and two 5GbE ports, and TOS covers backup, photos, and Docker. Its limits are single-lane M.2 slots, no ECC option, and details such as rubber feet that fall off. The UGREEN DXP2800 suits a small household that needs a mirrored pair and a modest Plex server, as long as it will not outgrow two bays.
 For homelab owners who want to install their own system, the choice is about processor and memory. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U is the lowest-cost route to eight cores and four bays, without hot-swap trays or NAS software. The Minisforum N5 Air adds a fifth bay, 10GbE, a PCIe slot, and a faster Ryzen chip. The Minisforum N5 Pro adds a 12-core chip, ECC support up to 96GB, and U.2, for owners who want one box for storage, virtual machines, and Jellyfin (Plex runs on its CPU cores, not its graphics). Plan on TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox on both Minisforum units, because MinisCloud OS is still immature.
 For large libraries and studios, the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus give six or eight bays, a Core i5, dual 10GbE, Thunderbolt 4, and a PCIe slot. Both are loud enough with full bays that they belong in a closet or office rather than beside a desk. For video and photo editors who want speed more than capacity, the all-flash UGREEN DXP480T Plus holds four M.2 SSDs in a small aluminum case with 10GbE and Thunderbolt 4, at a much higher cost per terabyte than hard drives.
 Whichever you pick, set up a second copy of your data on day one, on a USB drive, a second NAS, or cloud storage. The rest of our NAS coverage is on the NAS hub .

 A NAS without Intel QuickSync hands every stream your TV cannot play straight to the CPU. A four-core appliance gives up on the first 4K HDR file. That single spec decides the best NAS for Jellyfin more than bay count or brand, yet most spec sheets hide it behind phrases like “hardware transcoding engine”.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 169001 
 We narrowed the field to five boxes you can buy new on Amazon US today. Each chip was read against the Intel ARK spec pages and the Jellyfin hardware acceleration docs, including where Jellyfin support ends for Jasper Lake. Plex runs on all of them too, but a lifetime Plex Pass now costs $749.99, which is why Jellyfin leads this guide. This is a spec and capability guide, not a bench test: stock, prices and chip data were checked in October 2026 against the makers’ pages and live listings, so no stream count below is borrowed from an old benchmark.
 Top picks at a glance
 For most homes running Jellyfin or Plex, buy the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus . Its 12th-gen Intel chip has QuickSync with AV1 decode, it ships with 10GbE, and it takes any drive. Every pick in this table was in stock on Amazon US when we checked, and every one except the Synology transcodes in hardware.

 Best budget UGREEN NASync DXP2800 Intel N100 Yes, AV1 decode 2 + 2 M.2 about $370 to $390 
 Best for Plex with PCIe QNAP TS-664 Celeron N5095 Yes, no AV1 6 + 2 M.2 about $800 
 Best for DSM Synology DS925+ AMD Ryzen V1500B No iGPU 4 + 2 M.2 about $770 
 Two picks from the last version of this page are gone. The TerraMaster F4-425 Pro with the Core i3-N305 is out of stock, and its N350 replacement sells for about $800, more than the UGREEN four-bay with built-in 10GbE, so it no longer earns a value award. The eight-bay UGREEN DXP8800 Plus is also out of stock on Amazon, and our 8-bay NAS guide covers the large-library boxes you can still buy.
 How we picked these boxes
 None of these units sat in our rack for a month of streaming, and we will not pretend otherwise. Competing guides quote “10 simultaneous 4K streams” figures lifted from a years-old Plex PassMark rule of thumb. That rule says nothing about Jellyfin, HDR tone mapping or AV1. We checked the things a spec sheet can prove instead:
 The codename, graphics and QuickSync flag of every CPU match the Intel ARK page for that exact chip.
 Every codec claim traces to the Intel media driver codec table or to the Jellyfin hardware acceleration docs.
 The bays, M.2 slots, shipped RAM and network ports of every pick match the current product page from its maker.
 Every Amazon ASIN resolves to the exact diskless model and was in stock, sold new, on the day of the check.
 Every price is a band from that one reading, because NAS and drive prices are moving weekly before Black Friday.
 If a claim on this page could not be traced to one of those sources, we cut it. That is why you will not find a stream count here. The chip table below matters more than any award.
 Jellyfin transcode support by NAS chip
 Jellyfin transcodes in hardware on any Intel chip with QuickSync, but what it can decode, and how long that support lasts, depends on the graphics generation. The 12th-gen N-series and Alder Lake chips decode AV1 and handle HEVC 10-bit both ways. Jasper Lake handles HEVC 10-bit but has no AV1 at all, and Jellyfin is winding down its QuickSync path on Linux.

 Celeron N5095 QNAP TS-664 Jasper Lake Yes Yes / Yes No / No Linux QSV being deprecated, VA-API fallback

 Intel’s media driver lists Alder Lake-N by name but not Twin Lake. The starred N150 and N350 cells assume the same Gen 12 media block the rest of the N-series family shares. No chip in this table encodes AV1: the Jellyfin docs put AV1 encode on Arc graphics and Meteor Lake or newer. So any NAS here that advertises “AV1” means decode only, which is the half that matters when a client cannot play the file.
 Read the Jasper Lake row twice. The Jellyfin Intel hardware acceleration docs say Ice Lake, Jasper Lake and Elkhart Lake “are losing support for QSV on Linux” because Intel deprecated the MediaSDK runtime. They tell buyers to pick newer hardware. VA-API keeps those chips transcoding, and Jasper Lake also needs the i915 GuC setting for low-power encoding, so it works but carries more setup and less runway.
 HDR to SDR tone mapping runs in hardware on every Intel chip here, because they all decode HEVC 10-bit. Intel iGPUs also have no cap on simultaneous encode sessions, unlike consumer NVIDIA cards.
 Best overall for Jellyfin and Plex: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus covers every box a Jellyfin buyer needs to tick without a trade-off you’ll feel in year two. Its Pentium Gold 8505 is a 12th-gen Alder Lake chip with 48-EU UHD graphics, so QuickSync decodes AV1 and handles HEVC 10-bit with hardware tone mapping. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 64GB), four SATA bays plus two M.2 NVMe slots, and both a 10GbE and a 2.5GbE port.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: 4-bay, Pentium Gold 8505 with QuickSync, 10GbE and 2.5GbE, no drive lock. Image: UGREEN. 
 UGREEN ships Jellyfin as an App Center package on its Intel models, so there is no container to wire up by hand. UGOS Pro accepts any CMR drive and any NVMe with no compatibility list. If you outgrow the vendor OS, the x86 board boots TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid. It sells for about $630 to $660; check the live price .
 Buy it for files, backups, a few containers and a transcoding media server in one chassis. Pass on it if you want the Synology DSM ecosystem, or if two bays are honestly enough, in which case the DXP2800 below costs about $250 less.
 Best value QuickSync NAS: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus is the cheapest four-bay here that still decodes AV1 in hardware. Intel ARK lists its N95 as a four-core Alder Lake-N part with 16-EU UHD graphics and QuickSync. That puts it in the 12th-gen N series Jellyfin points low-power buyers toward. TerraMaster pairs it with 8GB of DDR4, four SATA bays, three M.2 NVMe slots and two 5GbE ports, and rates its transcoding engine for H.264 and H.265 up to 4K at 60fps.
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus: 4-bay, Intel N95 with QuickSync, three M.2 slots and dual 5GbE. Image: TerraMaster. 
 Graphics muscle is where it gives ground. Sixteen execution units is the smallest iGPU in this guide, a third of the DXP4800 Plus, so a household with several remote viewers tone-mapping 4K HDR at once will hit its ceiling first. Intel also rates the N95 for single-channel memory up to 16GB, so treat it as a media and backup box rather than a VM host. At about $510 it undercuts the UGREEN four-bay by roughly $120; check the live price .
 Buy it if one or two people stream at a time and you’d rather put the savings toward drives. Look elsewhere if you need 10GbE on one port, plan to run a pile of containers, or prefer the larger app catalogues of UGOS Pro, DSM or QTS over TerraMaster TOS.
 Best budget NAS for Jellyfin: UGREEN DXP2800
 The DXP2800 runs the Intel N100, the exact chip the Jellyfin hardware selection guide names as a recommended iGPU. That makes it the safest cheap entry into hardware transcoding. Its 24-EU graphics decode AV1 and HEVC 10-bit, and the box pairs two SATA bays with two M.2 NVMe slots, 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 16GB) and a 2.5GbE port.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: 2-bay, Intel N100 with QuickSync, 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 Cheap two-bays usually force a compromise here. The Synology DS225+ uses an Intel chip whose GPU driver Synology reportedly removed, so Synology Community users report it transcoding on the CPU. The DXP2800 avoids that and runs about $370 to $390; check the live price . Two bays fill faster than people expect, though. A mirrored pair gives you the space of one drive, so if your library is already past a few terabytes, a four-bay pick saves a second purchase. Our 2-bay NAS guide compares it with the other small boxes.
 Best for Plex with PCIe expansion: QNAP TS-664
 The TS-664 is the pick when Plex, not Jellyfin, is the media server and you want room to grow. Its Celeron N5095 is a Jasper Lake chip with QuickSync. The Plex support article on hardware streaming says NAS users need “JasperLake or better” to transcode to HEVC reliably, so the N5095 clears that bar. It ships with 8GB of RAM (16GB maximum), six SATA bays, two M.2 slots, two 2.5GbE ports, HDMI at 4K 60Hz and a PCIe Gen3 slot for a 10GbE card later.
 QNAP TS-664: 6-bay, Celeron N5095 with QuickSync and a PCIe Gen3 slot for 10GbE. Image: QNAP. 
 For Jellyfin this is the weakest Intel pick on the page. Jasper Lake has no AV1 decode, its Linux QSV path is the one Jellyfin is retiring, and QTS has no official Jellyfin package, so it runs through Container Station or a community package. At about $800 it also costs more than the DXP4800 Plus with built-in 10GbE; check the live price . Choose it for six bays and Plex, not for a long-lived Jellyfin server.
 Best for the DSM ecosystem: Synology DS925+
 The DS925+ cannot transcode video in hardware at all, because its AMD Ryzen V1500B has no integrated GPU. Every Jellyfin or Plex transcode lands on four CPU cores, which is fine for direct play to a capable client and poor for anything else. It earns a place for DSM, still the most polished NAS software, plus ECC memory and Synology’s backup suite.
 Synology DiskStation DS925+: 4-bay, AMD V1500B, DSM software, ECC RAM, no hardware transcoding. Image: Synology. 
 DSM 7.3 (October 2025) restored full support for third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs. Creating an M.2 NVMe storage pool still requires drives on the Synology compatibility list. The box ships with 4GB of ECC RAM (32GB maximum), which fills quickly once containers start, and runs about $770; check the live price .
 If your clients direct-play everything, it works. Our Synology NAS guide covers the rest of the range and why owners of the Intel DS225+ and DS425+ report the same transcoding problem.
 Plex Pass pricing versus free Jellyfin
 A new lifetime Plex Pass went from $249.99 to $749.99 on July 1, 2026, according to the Plex pricing announcement . The same change added a 5-Year pass at $249.99 and left monthly and annual pricing unchanged (reported at $6.99 and $69.99). Three Plex rules shape a NAS purchase:
 Hardware-accelerated streaming in Plex still requires an active Plex Pass on the server.
 Remote playback of your own video has required Plex Pass or a Remote Watch Pass ($2.99 a month) since April 29, 2025.
 Plex does not support hardware-accelerated streaming inside a virtual machine, so run it in Docker or natively on the NAS.
 Jellyfin charges nothing for hardware transcoding, remote access or extra users, so the NAS is the whole bill. The lifetime pass alone now costs more than the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus. If your household already pays for Plex Pass, every Intel box here serves it well; if you’re starting fresh, Jellyfin on the DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 avoids the subscription entirely.
 Container settings that keep QuickSync working
 The Jellyfin hardware selection guide warns that prebuilt NAS appliances can make third-party apps hard to install. The usual failure is a container that never sees the GPU, so every stream falls back to the CPU without an error. For the official jellyfin/jellyfin image on an Intel NAS, the Jellyfin Intel docs set three conditions:
 The container has the render node /dev/dri/renderD128 passed through from the host.
 The container runs with the render group ID of the host added (some releases use video instead).
 QSV or VA-API is selected under Dashboard, Playback, Transcoding, with the decode codecs your chip supports ticked.
 Kernel version is the other trap: the same docs note that 12th and 13th-gen Intel graphics need Linux kernel 6.2 or newer. That matters if you swap the vendor OS for an older distro. If you’d rather skip the appliance software entirely, our Jellyfin media server build uses an N150 board, and pairing any of these boxes with a streaming device that direct-plays cuts how often the NAS transcodes at all.
 Drives cost more than the box
 Every NAS here ships empty, and in 2026 the drives are usually the bigger bill. Four WD Red Plus 10TB drives, the value CMR pick in our best NAS hard drives guide , run about $460 each, so roughly $1,840 for a set, which is more than any four-bay on this page. Buy CMR, never SMR: the CMR vs SMR explainer shows how SMR drives stall RAID rebuilds. Expect both drive and RAM prices to keep moving while the memory and storage shortage lasts, which is also why the RAM a box ships with matters more than its upgrade ceiling.
 Black Friday NAS pricing to watch
 Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026 and Cyber Monday on November 30, and the NAS listings above already sit below their list prices. On the day we checked, Amazon showed the DXP4800 Plus, the DXP2800 and the DS925+ each about 13% to 14% under the list price on the listing. The F4-425 Plus showed a bigger cut against its Amazon list price, but TerraMaster’s own store listed it lower than that and out of stock, so Amazon was the only place we found it buyable. Before you call a holiday price a deal, check these conditions:
 The holiday price beats the current price band in the table above, not only the struck-through list price.
 The listing is the same diskless model and RAM configuration as the pick, not a bundle or a lower-RAM variant.
 The seller is the brand or Amazon, so the warranty and returns are straightforward.
 Drives tend to see the deeper cuts. Our Black Friday NAS and drive deals page tracks both through Cyber Monday.
 Which NAS fits your library
 Bay count and stream count decide this more than brand. Start from how much media you already own and how many people watch at once:
 One or two viewers, a library under about 8TB: the UGREEN DXP2800, or more two-bays in our 2-bay roundup .
 A family library with room to grow on a budget: the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus.
 A family library plus containers and fast copies from a desktop: the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, with more price tiers in the 4-bay NAS guide .
 Plex with six bays and a PCIe slot: the QNAP TS-664.
 A large library or several remote viewers: an eight-bay from our 8-bay NAS picks .
 Photo libraries run on the same boxes, and our NAS for Immich guide covers the extra RAM that machine learning needs. Live TV adds an HDHomeRun tuner for Plex and Jellyfin , and if none of the appliances fit, the DIY versus prebuilt comparison works through the costs of building your own.
 Pairs with Best UPS for Homelab and NAS (2026): Pure Sine Picks + NUT

 Pre-purchase transcode checklist
 Run these checks against any NAS listing before you buy, including ones not on this page. Each one is a condition the box must meet, and each traces to a source you can open yourself:
 The CPU is an Intel chip whose ARK page shows Intel Quick Sync Video as Yes.
 The Intel codename is Alder Lake, Alder Lake-N, Twin Lake or newer, not Jasper Lake, Elkhart Lake or Ice Lake, if Jellyfin is the main server.
 The chip decodes HEVC 10-bit, so HDR to SDR tone mapping runs on the GPU.
 The chip decodes AV1 if any of your files or downloads use it.
 The vendor ships Jellyfin as a package, or the NAS runs Docker with access to /dev/dri .
 The box ships with at least 8GB of RAM, because upgrades cost several times more than they did in June 2026.
 The listing is sold new by the brand or Amazon and matches the exact model number on the spec page from the maker.
 The drives you plan to fill it with are CMR and are priced into the same budget as the box.
